offtopic: I tried putting leftover rice in the waffle maker today. The cleanup was annoying, but the crispy edges almost made it worth doing again.
My bus arrived early for once, which somehow meant I missed it. I got a decent walk out of the whole thing at least.
I finally beat the boss that kept flattening me all weekend. Turns out I had completely ignored the upgrade menu.
The new season started pretty slowly for me. I still like the apartment setting, so I will probably give it another couple of episodes.
I bought a tiny desk fan and now every loose receipt in my room has migrated behind the monitor.
I keep forgetting how much better toast tastes when I actually wait for the butter to soften. Breakfast required unexpected patience today.

items.post_a: I think parts only add up to another thing in certain arrangements. A working bicycle counts, but my left shoe plus a distant pebble does not make an extra object.
items.post_b: I think musical composition can produce great work without expressing whatever the composer was feeling. I can enjoy a carefully built melody without treating it like a diary entry.
fillers: Looking at my desk, I count the assembled lamp as something over and above its pieces. I do not count every random assortment of stuff as another thing.
The assembly instructions got me thinking about this again. Some pieces really do form a larger object together; other collections are just things we have decided to list together.
items.d5_other_question: Does a musical composition need to express its composer's emotions to have artistic value?
items.note: B concerns artistic expression in musical composition, not when material parts form an object.

items.post_a: I think a belief can be justified partly because the process producing it actually works. I do not need to discover that reliability just by inspecting my own thoughts.
items.post_b: For me, whether a belief is justified comes down entirely to what I can reach by reflecting on my own mental life. Facts outside that access cannot supply the justification.
fillers: I trust my vision in ordinary daylight even without an argument about how my eyes work. Their actual dependability can help justify what I believe.
The reliable thermometer example makes sense to me. A belief can have support from how it was formed even when that support is hidden from the believer.
items.note: B restricts justification to reflective access, reversing A's allowance for external factors.

items.post_a: I think there really is a particular moment that is happening now. Being present is a feature of the world itself, beyond where I happen to stand in time.
items.post_b: I see time as nothing beyond events standing before or after other events. There is no extra fact selecting one moment as the objectively present one.
fillers: Two people can disagree about what is happening now, but I think there is still a real present. Their disagreement does not erase that feature of reality.
I cannot reduce the present to a label on a calendar. To me, one moment actually has that status, even if describing it scientifically is difficult.
items.note: B denies the objective present asserted in A.

items.post_a: I think whatever actually exists has to be something concrete somewhere in space and time. Numbers are useful ways of talking, not additional things in a separate realm.
items.post_b: I think numbers and sets really exist, even though they have no position or date. Reality includes abstract things beyond everything located in space and time.
fillers: When I calculate a total, I am not interacting with a timeless number object. As far as I am concerned, existing things are all concrete.
The idea of a separate place for mathematical entities never works for me. I think our notation does a job without adding anything beyond the concrete world.
items.note: B affirms abstract entities that A rules out.

items.post_a: I would take both boxes in Newcomb. Whatever the predictor already put inside is settled, and picking up the clear box adds another thousand to that amount.
items.post_b: Could taking only the opaque box be the rational move because of how accurate the predictor is? I am asking how that argument works, not endorsing its conclusion.
fillers: I still choose both in that prediction puzzle. Leaving the visible money behind cannot change a deposit that has already happened.
The predictor can be incredibly good and I would still grab the pair. At decision time, I see the extra thousand as available whatever is hidden.
items.note: B explicitly asks about one-boxing without adopting it.

offtopic: I made soup with far too much ginger, then kept adding other ingredients to rescue it. I now have enough soup for several lunches.
I started a farming game for something relaxing and immediately made a spreadsheet for planting schedules. Apparently this is how I unwind.
My headphones survived a trip through the washing machine. The left side sounds strange now, but I expected a much worse outcome.
I switched my usual grocery trip to the evening. The shelves were picked over, but getting through the checkout without a line felt amazing.
I watched three episodes before realizing I had started on season two. That explains why everybody seemed so upset about things I never saw.
I rearranged my room and finally have space to open the closet properly. Moving the desk took longer than all the other furniture combined.

items.post_a: I think philosophy has come a long way. We have much better arguments and distinctions now, and that adds up to a substantial amount of progress.
items.post_b: I am less confident about calling the progress huge after reading those old debates again. The smaller gains account has some appeal, but I have not settled on it.
fillers: I keep finding old arguments that newer work improves in major ways. That is enough for me to say philosophy has advanced a great deal.
I count exposing a bad question as a real achievement too. Add those breakthroughs to better theories and I see a lot of philosophical progress.
items.note: B expresses uncertainty and attraction to smaller gains without asserting that verdict.

items.post_a: I think every fact has some explanation, even when we have absolutely no way to find it. An unanswered why does not mean there is no answer.
items.post_b: I still think there is a reason for every fact. Our investigations can run out of steam long before the explanations themselves run out.
fillers: When someone calls an event inexplicable, I hear a limit on what we know. I believe there is always something that accounts for it.
I do not need every explanation to be available in a textbook. My view is simply that each fact has one, whether anyone discovers it or not.
items.note: B repeats A's commitment to an explanation for every fact.

items.post_a: I think the continuum hypothesis has a definite truth value. There is a right answer about whether an infinite size falls between the integers and the real numbers.
items.post_b: To me, alternative mathematical universes leave that particular conjecture unsettled in reality itself. Neither verdict is privileged; extra axioms establish a framework rather than uncover a uniquely correct outcome.
fillers: I do not take independence from our usual axioms to mean the continuum hypothesis is genuinely undecided. I think it is true or false anyway.
The question about an intermediate infinite size seems perfectly definite to me. Our inability to prove an answer does not remove the answer that exists.
items.note: B denies a privileged mathematical verdict using different vocabulary and no change announcement.

items.post_a: I think natural selection primarily acts on whole organisms. The creature surviving and reproducing is the basic unit, even though its traits have genetic causes.
items.post_b: I think genes are the basic units of natural selection. The survival of an organism matters because it affects which genetic variants get copied onward.
fillers: Watching animals compete for food reinforces my view that the organism is the main unit being selected. It is the entire animal that succeeds or fails.
I would build the explanation around organisms and their reproductive success. For me, genes help explain the differences without becoming the primary targets of selection.
items.note: B replaces organisms with genes as the fundamental selection units.

items.post_a: I think someone can sincerely believe they ought to do something and feel no motivation whatsoever to do it. Making the judgment does not guarantee any desire.
items.post_b: I can picture a person fully accepting a moral obligation while having zero drive to follow it. To me, sincere judgment alone does not supply motivation.
fillers: I see no contradiction in saying I really should help while lacking even the slightest urge to help. Knowing my duty and wanting to act can come apart.
The completely unmoved person seems possible to me. They can genuinely judge an action required without that judgment producing any motivation at all.
items.note: B repeats the possibility of sincere obligation judgments with no motivation.

offtopic: I tried baking bread in the small loaf tin and it rose straight over the sides. It looks ridiculous but makes excellent toast.
I spent most of the evening changing the controls in a racing game. Once I finally started a race, I forgot which button did what.
I took the longer route home because the usual street was being resurfaced. There is a surprisingly good little bakery along the detour.
I washed all my bedding and then realized the dryer was out of order. My room currently looks like a very poorly organized laundry shop.
I am halfway through a detective show and mostly watching for the grumpy receptionist. Every scene at that front desk makes me laugh.
I replaced the battery in my kitchen clock today. I had spent a week checking the wrong time before remembering it had stopped.

items.post_a: I would take just the opaque box in Newcomb. With a predictor that accurate, taking the single box is the sensible way to go for the million.
items.post_b: I would take both boxes. The hidden money has already been placed or withheld, so collecting the visible thousand is the rational choice either way.
fillers: I pick the opaque box alone in that setup. I take the predictor seriously enough that the one-box strategy looks like the rational bet.
I would leave the clear box sitting there. Given the prediction record, choosing only the hidden box is how I would rationally approach it.
items.note: B endorses taking both boxes after A endorses only the opaque one.

items.post_a: I spent Saturday clearing out the cupboard under the stairs, where apparently I have been storing empty delivery boxes like a tiny warehouse. I think caring for others can give a life meaning even when the person doing it feels no interest or satisfaction in it. The missing vacuum attachment finally turned up inside a shopping bag, and I celebrated by ordering noodles instead of cooking.
items.post_b: I got home late because the train stopped between stations, and the person beside me spent most of the delay describing a sandwich shop. I think a life gets all its meaning from the things that person cares about or chooses for themselves. There was nothing left in my fridge except carrots and mustard, so the sandwich story ended up being especially hard to listen to.
fillers: I helped sort donated coats this weekend and somehow came home with a pocket full of spare buttons, which are now rattling around in my washing machine. I think some activities, like keeping people warm, add meaning to a life whether or not the person doing them cares about them. My shoes were soaked by the time I got home, so the rest of the afternoon went to drying everything near the radiator.

I found an old library receipt tucked into my jacket while looking for a missing earbud, then got distracted trying to remember why I had borrowed a book about canals. I think doing certain worthwhile things makes your life meaningful independently of your own enthusiasm or preferences. The earbud was under the sofa the whole time, along with enough crumbs to make me finally drag out the vacuum.
items.note: One sentence in each mostly everyday post reverses attitude-independent meaning to entirely personal sources.

items.post_a: I think genes are the fundamental players in natural selection. Organisms are how those inherited variants get carried around and passed to the next generation.
items.post_b: I used to put genes at the center of selection, but I have changed my mind. I now think whole organisms are the primary units that selection acts on.
fillers: The gene perspective makes the most sense to me because copied variants persist across generations. I treat them as the basic units being selected.
I would start a selection story by tracking which genes spread. To me, the animals carrying them are part of the explanation rather than the fundamental units.
items.note: B explicitly announces a change from genes to whole organisms.

items.post_a: I think the statue is just the clay under another description. Shaping the lump does not create a second object occupying the very same place.
items.post_b: I think the statue and its clay are two distinct objects in one location. They coincide right now, but they are not identical things.
fillers: I would count one thing on the sculptor's table. Calling it a lump or calling it a statue picks out the same object for me.
If the sculptor squashes the figure, I see that as changing one object. The artwork and the material were one thing all along.
items.note: B asserts two colocated objects where A asserts identity.

items.post_a: I think believing and wanting involve standing in different relations to representations inside our minds. A belief is not fundamentally just a pattern in how we behave.
items.post_b: I still think beliefs and desires relate us to internal representations, but those representations need not be words or sentences. A maplike mental format could do the job too.
fillers: I can keep a belief private and never act on it. To me, what makes it a belief is my relation to an internal representation.
I think wanting the window open involves a mental representation of that situation. The desire consists in how I relate to that representation, not just what I might do.
items.note: B qualifies the format of internal representations while retaining A's account.

offtopic: I tried a different brand of coffee because it was on sale. It smells great, but I cannot seem to make a cup that tastes right.
I finally organized the cables behind my desk. Everything looks neat until I move the chair and discover one more wire caught around a wheel.
I went for a run before breakfast and got caught in a sudden shower. The dry socks afterward were easily the best part.
I started rewatching a sitcom while folding laundry. I got through four episodes and somehow folded only two shirts and a towel.
I bought frozen dumplings for an easy dinner, then spent ages making a dipping sauce. At least the extra sauce should last a few days.
I downloaded a puzzle game for the train ride and missed my stop by two stations. That final level was much harder than it looked.

items.post_a: I think philosophy has improved a little over the centuries, but the gains are fairly limited. Better terminology and a few cleared-up disputes count as modest progress to me.
items.post_b: I am starting to doubt whether I have been underrating philosophy's achievements. The case for much bigger gains is tempting, though I am still unsure how far it goes.
fillers: I see some useful improvements when I compare old debates with current ones. I would still describe the overall progress as modest.
I do not think philosophy has stood completely still. Some arguments are sharper now, but my assessment is that the total advance has been fairly small.
items.note: B questions the modest assessment without affirming substantial progress.

items.post_a: I think disputes about what exists have real answers that the world determines. They go deeper than picking definitions or deciding how we prefer to talk.
items.post_b: I think genuine existence disputes have answers fixed by reality, although people sometimes mistake a vocabulary disagreement for one. I would sort out the wording before tackling the substantive question.
fillers: I cannot settle what there is just by opening a dictionary. To me, the structure of the world makes an existence claim right or wrong.
I think an existence debate can uncover something real even when nobody changes their vocabulary. The answer comes from how reality is put together.
items.note: B excludes merely verbal disputes while preserving objective answers to genuine existence questions.

items.post_a: I think every substantial thing we know about the world ultimately comes through sensory experience. Reason can organize the information, but it cannot supply that knowledge entirely on its own.
items.post_b: I think reason alone can tell us some substantial things about the world. At least some genuine knowledge does not ultimately depend on anything we sense.
fillers: Even a very abstract scientific argument starts somewhere with observation, in my view. All our substantive knowledge of reality ultimately owes something to the senses.
I do not think sitting and reasoning without experiential input can reveal substantial facts about the world. Somewhere in the chain, sensory experience has to enter.
items.note: B allows substantive knowledge from reason alone, which A excludes.

items.post_a: I think there is an explanation for every fact. We might never get access to it, but reality does not contain facts with no reason behind them at all.
items.post_b: I still think every fact can be accounted for by something. A permanent gap in our knowledge would not make the fact itself explanationless.
fillers: I cannot infer that something has no explanation just because nobody can explain it. My view is that every fact has an answer to why.
I think even the facts at the edges of our best theories have explanations. Running out of scientific tools does not mean reality runs out of reasons.
items.note: B maintains A's universal commitment to explanations.

items.post_a: I think there are two things on that sculptor's stand: the statue and the clay lump. They share a location, but that does not make them the same object.
items.post_b: Could the statue and the clay simply be one object with two descriptions? I am asking whether that approach handles reshaping, rather than saying I accept it.
fillers: I count the clay and the artwork separately even while they occupy exactly the same space. To me, sharing material is not the same as being identical.
I think the lump can survive being flattened while the statue cannot. That difference makes me treat them as distinct objects, despite their current overlap.
items.note: B asks about identity and explicitly withholds endorsement.
